title: Obedient Unto Death (Mark 14:32–52)
description: The King Who Chose to Die: Obedient Unto Death
transcript: They went to a place called Gethsemane, and Jesus said to his disciples, 'Sit here while I pray.' He took Peter, James, and John along with him, and he began to be deeply distressed and troubled. 'My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death,' he said to them. 'Stay here and keep watch.' Going a little farther, he fell to the ground and prayed that if possible the hour might pass from him. 'Abba, Father,' he said, 'everything is possible for you. Take this cup from me, yet not what I will, but what you will.' Then he returned to his disciples and found them sleeping. 'Simon,' he said to Peter, 'are you asleep? Couldn't you keep watch for one hour?' Watch and pray so that you will not fall into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. Once more he went away and prayed the same thing. When he came back, he again found them sleeping because their eyes were heavy. They did not know what to say to him. Returning the third time, he said to them, are you still sleeping and resting? 'Enough! The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is delivered into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go. Here comes my betrayer.' Just as he was speaking, Judas, one of the 12, appeared. With him was a crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests, the teachers of the law, and the elders. Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them. 'The one I kiss is the man. Arrest him and lead him away under guard.' Going at once to Jesus, Judas said, 'Rabbi,' and kissed him. The men seized Jesus and arrested him. Then one of those standing near drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear. 'Am I leading a rebellion,' said Jesus, 'that you have come out with swords and clubs to capture me?' 'Every day I was with you teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest me. But the scriptures must be fulfilled.' Then everyone deserted him and fled. A young man wearing nothing but a linen garment was following Jesus. When they seized him, he fled naked, leaving his garment behind. You have to go out, but you don't have to come back. That was the unofficial, rather stark motto of the United States Lifesaving Service in the 19th century, which then became the US Coast Guard as it is today. And I've seen or heard the same sentiment echoed in the British National Lifeboat Institution about courageous people who go out to sea to rescue people in danger when ships are in danger. You have to go out. Not because you're forced to, because almost all those who do go out in lifeboats are volunteers, but they've made a choice when there's no other choice. That is, if lives are to be saved at all, then you have to go out. But you don't have to come back, and you might not, for if lives are to be saved, it may cost you your own. Well, what's that all got to do with our reading that we've just heard this evening? Well, what I want us to suggest for our reflection is that the two halves of our reading express two great truths. One, Jesus didn't have to die, but he did choose to. But on the other hand, Jesus did have to die, for there was no other choice if lives were to be saved, including yours and mine. So here we are then in this 14th chapter of Mark's Gospel, and all the way through, Mark has been showing us who Jesus really was. On the one hand, of course, he was a real man. He was the son of a carpenter from Nazareth, just as fully human as any of us. But he is also— right from the very first verse of Mark's Gospel, he is described as Jesus the Messiah, the Son of God. And those two truths about Jesus—man and Messiah, Son of a carpenter, Son of God—are the key to both parts, both halves of the text that we've just heard read. In Gethsemane, we see Jesus the man submitting himself to the will of God his Father. And in his arrest, in the second half of the passage, we see Jesus the Messiah submitting himself to the word of God in his scriptures. So first of all then, let's look at how Jesus the man, Jesus submits himself to the will of God his Father. And you can see there in verses 33 to 34, the agony that he's in. It's pretty dramatic, isn't it? The way our text describes Jesus. And his state of mind, three very powerful words: he was deeply distressed, he was troubled, overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death. I mean, what's going on? Well, Jesus was facing death by crucifixion, you might say, in a few hours' time. And wouldn't you be pretty troubled if that's what you were facing? Well, yes, of course. But then this hasn't all just, you know, come out of the blue all of a sudden. I mean, Jesus has already been predicting his violent death 3 times already in this Gospel. He had set his face to go to Jerusalem, we read, and he knew perfectly well what's going to happen there. Plus, he would have seen people crucified. I mean, everybody had seen crucifixions in those days. So he had, if you like, he had got plenty of time to get himself, so to speak, psyched up for it. I mean, after all, people have been able to face up to imminent death even in the most horrible ways, like being burnt at the stake and so on, with courage and with composure. I mean, wouldn't that have been a bit more heroic of Jesus? But no, you see, it wasn't just the fear of the physical agonies that made Jesus fall on his face to the ground in tears and sweat and cries. Although knowing what crucifixion is like We wouldn't blame him if that had been really what it was all about. The clue really for what is happening here is in those words of Jesus where he says, "Take this cup from me," he says, he prays to his Father. And what is this cup? Because in this same chapter, just a few hours ago, perhaps even less than an hour ago, Jesus had taken another cup, a literal cup, the cup of wine that he said was his blood that was being poured out for many. —the cup that we sometimes raise in the communion service, the cup of the blood of Jesus, the cup of salvation. But this cup that Jesus is referring to here, this is the cup that is brimming over with the just, righteous wrath of God against all sin, evil, and injustice in the world. This was the cup of judgement. The cup of condemnation. The cup which in the Old Testament the psalmists and the prophets had spoken about in pretty terrifying terms. Here, for example, is one quote from just one psalm which refers to it, Psalm 75: "In the hand of the Lord is a cup full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out, and all the wicked of the earth drink it down to its very dregs." And here is Jesus, the Son of God, God himself actually in human flesh, who is going to drink the cup of God's own anger against the sin of the whole world. And in doing so, the Son was going to go through that severing, wrenching abandonment from his Father. That was the shuddering horror that made him fall to the ground. That was the agony that of what he knew he was facing. But what then did he actually pray from that awful place on the ground? And that leads us therefore to the choice that he had to make. What was the choice? What did he actually pray for as he was prone on the ground? And we read his words, "Abba, Father," he said, "everything is possible for you." There it is in verse 35, 36, "Take this cup from me." 'Yet not what I will, but what you will, Father.'" So what's going on here? Is this a clash of wills between, within somehow, God himself, between the Son and the Father? Well, no, not at all. But we do have to think very carefully about who it is who is saying these words. Remember, as I emphasized a little earlier, this is Jesus' the man. This is Jesus the Son of God in his incarnate humanity, with a fully human nature and human will, in union, of course, with his fully divine nature and divine will. One person, but fully human and fully divine. And that's what's crucial at this moment. Because you see, it's in his humanity that Jesus here is wrestling with what he has come to do. I mean, as any sane human being would. Suffering, rejection, mockery, abandonment, torture, death, and in all of that bearing the weight of our sin, the world's sin, God's wrath. I mean, of course he doesn't want that. If only there could have been any other way. That's a perfectly human reaction. And Jesus was indeed perfectly human. Actually, Jesus had been wrestling with this from the very start. I mean, just think about it for a moment. Just about everybody in the Gospel story tried to get Jesus to go some other way than this. Father, please take it away." But nevertheless. You see, this is what I meant by saying that Jesus didn't have to die, in the sense that he was not forced to. Jesus wasn't the victim of some cosmic child abuse or some kind of parental coercive control or something like that. I mean, right up to the end, he was obedient unto death. This was the choice that Jesus had been making all the way through, man and boy, day after day, year after year. And now on the stony ground in a garden in the darkness in the early hours of the morning of that Friday, he is making that choice. But then we remember that man on the ground is none other than God the Son. And when he speaks to his Abba Father and says, "Your will be done," there is no conflict between the Father and the Son because, you see, the will of the Father was also the will of the Son and the will of the Holy Spirit from all eternity. You see, what is going to happen here this very day, this Friday, after the sun rises, had been planned by God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together. Before the sun even existed or this planet Earth. According to Revelation, Jesus is, quote, "the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world." This moment, the cross of Christ, had been in the plan of God from all eternity. And now it is the Son in his incarnation, the Son who has taken on our human flesh in order to accomplish the work of salvation within history, it's the human Son who submits himself to the Father. This earthly submission and obedience is not part of the Father-Son relationship as God is eternally in himself, in the Holy Trinity. This is the willing choice of the incarnate Son in his earthly life, and he's doing it for our salvation. I think that's what the writer to the Hebrews meant when he speaks in this passage, which almost certainly is referring to Gethsemane, where he says that during the days of Jesus' life on earth, his earthly life, he offered up prayers and petitions with fervent cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission, Son though he was, He learned obedience from what he suffered, which of course doesn't mean that he had been disobedient before he suffered. No, what it means is that his obedience to his Father on earth was a chosen, experienced part of his human nature in which he suffered for our salvation. Jesus didn't have to die; he chose to. He had chosen to in all eternity and now in time, this time, this hour, this very day. That is the choice he made. And we are really just only scratching the surface of what it meant for him. And the question is, what might it mean for us? It is very hard to even imagine how to apply something like this if that is what we are wanting to do. But what does it mean for us to submit our will to God's will. And yet, you know, isn't that what we do every time we say the Lord's Prayer? I mean, unless of course we think that when we say the words, "Your will be done on earth as in heaven," we imagine that it doesn't really include us or apply to us, whereas actually of course it does. And what is happening here is that Jesus was simply doing exactly what he told us to pray. Which is that God's will should be done in his life and in ours. There isn't time to go into what that might mean for any of us. I have to leave that really for you to think about and to wonder and to ponder with the help of the Holy Spirit what that submission to the will of God for your life might mean. But what about those disciples? Let's go back to them in our story, back there, especially to those 3 of them who were close enough to have heard Jesus' cries and prayers. At least before they fell asleep, that is. I mean, after all, the Passover was quite a big meal. There was lots of wine and it was the middle of the night, so we can't blame them too much, I suppose. And I think actually that Jesus goes back to them these 3 times not so much because he's desperate for their support as because he's concerned for them. That's what his words actually suggest, I think, that they were facing a severe test a testing which they would undoubtedly fail. Now at this point I have to say that normally when we're preaching from the Gospels, we do try to stick to the text of the Gospel we were in, in this case Mark. But just sometimes, and here I think it does help to hear one of the other Gospels. And in Matthew's account of this moment, what Jesus actually says at this point is quite staggering.
